A constant load, a healthy bank at nameplate capacity and a nominal temperature are assumed. Capacity falls with age and with cold — roughly 20 % at 0 °C for lead-acid — so a design should carry margin beyond this figure.
Depth of discharge protects battery life, not the calculation. Taking a lead-acid bank below about 50 % shortens its service life sharply; lithium tolerates 80–90 %.
System efficiency covers the inverter and wiring. The bank supplies more power than the load receives, which is why the discharge current is higher than load power over bank voltage.

A battery's capacity is only valid at the rate it was measured at. Discharge it harder and you get less than the nameplate amp-hours. The naive t = C / I ignores this and overestimates runtime — sometimes by a third at high rates.
A capacity figure without its rate is meaningless. 100 Ah at C/1 describes a far stronger cell than 100 Ah at C/20, which is why the rate is a required input.
The rate the capacity was measured at: 20 for C/20, common on lead-acid

Metric conduit is named by its outside diameter, so a 20 mm conduit has a bore nearer 17 mm. Take the internal figure from the manufacturer's data; using the nominal size overstates the space by about a third.
Passing this check does not remove the grouping derating. Cables bunched in a conduit carry less current than the same cables in free air — size them with the cable size calculator.
NEC Chapter 9, Table 1: 53 % for a single cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. The step down at two is not an error — two circles pack badly inside a third, so the usable fraction drops.
Length and bends matter as much as area. A long run with several bends may be impractical at the permitted fill; add a draw box rather than forcing the pull.

IEC 61386 is a product standard for conduit systems and sets no fill percentage. BS 7671 and the IET On-Site Guide use cable and conduit factors instead, which already account for the run's length and bends. Use the custom limit to work to either.

The limit is about installing the cable, not fitting it. A bundle has to slide past bends without the sheath being torn, and needs air around it to shed heat. An over-filled conduit is one that either cannot be pulled or cooks what is inside it.

No tabulated cross-section satisfies these inputs. Consider conductors in parallel, a shorter run, or a higher permitted voltage drop.
Tabulated capacities assume a single circuit at 30 °C. Ambient temperature and grouping factors are applied on top; six circuits bunched together lose about 43 % of their rating.
This calculator sizes the conductor only. Coordination with the protective device (Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz) and the disconnection time for fault protection must be checked separately.

Capacities follow the reference installation methods of IEC 60364-5-52 Annex B. Verify against the edition or national adoption that applies to your project, and against the cable manufacturer's data.

A cable must satisfy two independent requirements: carry the current without overheating, and deliver usable voltage at the load. The answer is the larger of the two sizes. Sizing on voltage drop alone can return a conductor that overheats.
Voltage drop is evaluated at the insulation's maximum conductor temperature, which is the worst case. Reactance is neglected, as in the voltage drop calculator.

Steel wire or tape armour is not included and adds substantially — often half the cable's mass again. Use the datasheet figure for armoured cable.
Add the drum for transport and lifting. A wooden drum for a kilometre of LV cable is itself in the order of 100–300 kg.

The complete-cable figure is an estimate. Insulation thickness is the manufacturer's choice, so the section that is not conductor is treated as solid compound of the chosen type. Against catalogue data this lands within a few percent.
The conductor figure is exact: one mm² of copper weighs 8.89 kg per kilometre, aluminium 2.70 kg. This is what a cable schedule quotes and what scrap is priced on.
Cable tray and ladder are rated in kg per metre of span. Compare the per-metre figure against the tray's rating with every cable it carries added together.

This is the energy charge alone. Standing charges, capacity charges, reactive energy and taxes are billed separately and are not in this figure.
Running hours dominate. A load's cost is decided by how long it runs far more than by what it draws, which is why the annual hours are shown as their own step.
Simple payback ignores the cost of money, the tariff changing and the alternative failing early. It is what a proposal is judged on, not an investment appraisal.

Zs: %1$s Ω of a permitted %2$s Ω
Z_s = Z_e + R₁ + R₂\nZ_s,max = c · U₀ / I_a\nS ≥ √(I² · t) / k

IEC 60364-5-54 permits two routes for the protective conductor: the calculation shown here, or the table rule (S ≤ 16 → S, 16–35 → 16, above 35 → S/2). Both are reported. The table is quicker and usually the larger conductor; either satisfies the standard.

The device's curve decides as much as the cable does. A Type C needs ten times its rating to trip where a Type B needs five, so it needs half the loop impedance. The same cable, the same length, a different breaker — and a circuit that passed now fails.

The k values are for a protective conductor incorporated in a cable or bunched with cables, from IEC 60364-5-54 Table 54.3. A conductor run separately is allowed a higher final temperature and a larger k; using these for that case is safe but not the right table.

The everyday failure is length. A run can be correct on current-carrying capacity and correct on voltage drop and still leave the device unable to see a fault at its far end. That is why this check is separate from cable sizing rather than folded into it.
Ze and the finished Zs should both be measured, not only calculated. A computed loop assumes every connection is sound; the measurement is what proves it.

A residual current device is judged differently: it responds to the imbalance between line and neutral, not to the size of the fault current, so the criterion is touch voltage — Zs × IΔn ≤ 50 V. A 30 mA device tolerates about 1667 Ω, which is why a TT installation works at all.

R₁ and R₂ are taken at the insulation's rated temperature, not at 20 °C. A fault is most likely on a warm cable, and a warm cable has the highest resistance and therefore the lowest fault current. Computing them cold flatters the answer in exactly the direction that matters.

A circuit needs both verdicts. Disconnection asks whether enough current flows to operate the device. Withstand asks whether the protective conductor survives the energy that flows while it does. A cable can pass the first and fail the second, which is how an installation clears its fault and melts its earth in the same instant.
Does not disconnect — Zs above the %1$s Ω limit

An EV draws its full current for hours. None of the diversity habits that make a socket circuit work carry over, which is why the simultaneity factor starts at one and is asked for rather than assumed.

A vehicle can put smooth DC into the protective conductor, which saturates the core of a Type A RCD and blinds it to the AC fault it was installed for. Either a Type B, or a Type A alongside a device that trips at 6 mA of DC — which most modern chargers have built in, but only if the plate says so.
Load management is not modelled. A controller that shares a fixed supply between points makes the design current a setting rather than a sum.
Type A, alongside the charger’s own 6 mA detection
One means no diversity, which is the honest starting point: charging is a continuous load. Lowering it is a decision about this site.
Three lines carry the same spectrum
Triplen harmonics add in the neutral only when all three lines produce them together. On a mixed board the neutral cannot be worked out from one line.

Cable derating is not included. IEC 60364-5-52 Annex E bands its reduction factors on third-harmonic content; those bands are transcribed figures, and everything shown here is derived and checked on every build.
Not available on an unbalanced board
Spectrum, as a percentage of the fundamental
The neutral carries more than the lines it serves. This is not a fault — it is what triplen harmonics do, and it is why a neutral sized as half the phase burns.

Light left after dirt and lamp ageing. 0,8 for a clean interior.
The lumen method gives an average over the working plane. It says nothing about uniformity, glare or what happens at the edges of the room — all of which a real lighting design has to answer.
Mounting height is measured above the working plane, not above the floor. Using the ceiling height is the most common way the room index comes out wrong.
The suggested layout is the pair of factors closest to square. Spacing, not count, is what decides uniformity.
The count is rounded up. Rounding 4,2 down to 4 is a design that misses its own target by 5 %.
The utilisation factor is specific to the luminaire, the room proportions and the surface reflectances. Take it from the manufacturer's table against the room index this calculator reports.
Rounded up; the achieved level is at or above the target
Room index, for looking up the utilisation factor
From the luminaire's own table, against the room index below. Typically 0,4 – 0,7.

From the motor plate. Six is typical; seven and eight are not unusual.

The cable between transformer and motor is not counted, so the dip at the motor itself is deeper than this. Neither is the star-delta transition peak, which can approach the direct-on-line current for a few cycles.

Torque follows the square of the voltage at the terminals, on top of whatever the starting method already gives up. A gentler start is not free: a method that thirds the current also thirds the pull, and a loaded machine may fail to turn.
Four per cent is usual up to about 630 kVA. Zero means an infinite bus.
Contactor coils may release at this depth. A start that takes the rest of the board with it is not a start.
Deep enough to be seen in the lighting.

On a DC supply there is no phase angle, so power factor is ignored and there is no reactive component.
Efficiency and power factor are both full load values. Both fall substantially at part load, so this result does not describe a lightly loaded motor.
Where the nameplate states a rated current, prefer it over a calculated value: it reflects the actual machine rather than assumed efficiency and power factor.

A motor's nameplate rating is its mechanical output at the shaft, not the electrical power it draws. The input is larger by the efficiency, so omitting that division under-reports the current by 8–15 % — enough to undersize a cable or a protective device.
Starting current is the steady-state locked rotor value. The initial peak includes a DC transient and is higher; motor protection and voltage dip studies need that peak, not this figure.
Nameplate shaft output, not electrical input
Line current at rated shaft output

Of the line current. Zero for a linear load; 30 – 70 % on a board full of electronics.
On a balanced linear circuit the line currents cancel in the neutral, which is why the neutral is traditionally the smallest conductor in the cable.
IEC 60364-5-52 requires the neutral to be counted as a loaded conductor once third-harmonic content passes 15 %, and the cable derated accordingly.
Measure the harmonic content with a true-RMS instrument. A mean-reading clamp under-reads distorted current, which is exactly the case you are trying to find.
The two contributions are at different frequencies, so they combine in quadrature. Adding them arithmetically would overstate the neutral by a wide margin.
The third harmonic and its multiples arrive in phase and add up instead. A perfectly balanced board can put three times one line's third-harmonic current into the neutral.
The neutral carries more than any line — treat it as a loaded conductor and derate the cable

Correction adds reactive power without changing active power. P is the fixed side of the triangle; only Q and S move, which is why the same work is done with less current.
Delta is usual at low voltage because it needs a third of the capacitance, though each unit must withstand the full line-to-line voltage.

This sizes a fixed bank for the stated load. Real installations vary, so automatic stepped correction is normal — a fixed bank sized for peak over-compensates at light load and can push the power factor leading, which some tariffs also penalise.
Harmonics are not considered. On a distorted supply, capacitors can resonate with the supply inductance and amplify harmonic currents; detuned reactors are required in that case.
The released capacity is usually what justifies the project: freeing apparent power in the transformer and cabling can defer a supply upgrade entirely.

cos φ alone does not say whether the current lags or leads. The magnitude is the same either way, but the sign of reactive power is opposite — which decides whether capacitors should be added or removed.
For three phase, enter the line-to-line voltage and the line current. The result is the total for all three phases.
Sinusoidal, balanced quantities are assumed. On a distorted supply the apparent power also carries a distortion component and S² = P² + Q² no longer holds; that case needs true-RMS measurement.
Many tariffs bill reactive energy against a tan φ threshold rather than cos φ. A tan φ of 0.20 corresponds to cos φ ≈ 0.98.
The three powers form a right triangle: S² = P² + Q². Apparent power is what the supply, cabling and switchgear must be rated for, even though only the active component does work.
Real power delivered to the load
Apparent power from the measured quantities

Returns through the neutral, so the loop is longer and the current lower. Decides whether the device trips at all.
The largest current a device may interrupt. Selects breaking capacity.
Z_s = c · U / (k · I_s)\nR = ρ(θ) · L / (A · n)\nI = c · U / (k · (Z_s + √(R² + X²)))
A reduced neutral raises the loop impedance and lowers the fault current

A line–neutral fault returns through the neutral, so both conductors are in the loop and the current is roughly half the three-phase figure. A reduced neutral makes it lower still. This is the fault that fails to trip, not the three-phase one.

A fault current on its own proves nothing. Compare the minimum against the current that operates the device in the required time, and check that the protective conductor survives the let-through energy. Both are in the Earth Fault Loop calculator.
If the supply is a transformer with no upstream network figure, the Transformer calculator gives the current at its terminals — but that value assumes an infinite bus and is only a starting point.

Supply and cable impedances are added as magnitudes, which is what loop impedance testers and IEC 60364 practice do. Their angles differ — a transformer-fed supply is mostly reactive, an LV cable mostly resistive — so the sum slightly overstates the loop and the current comes out a little low. That is the safe direction for verifying disconnection. Close to the origin, where breaking capacity is being selected, use a full IEC 60909 study.

Copper gains about 20 % resistance between 20 °C and its 70 °C PVC rating, and about 27 % at the 90 °C XLPE rating. On a long run that alone separates the two currents by more than the voltage factors do.

Two currents come out because two decisions need them, and using one where the other belongs is the mistake this calculator exists to prevent. The maximum (c = 1.05, conductor cold) is the most a device may have to interrupt. The minimum (c = 0.95, conductor at its rated temperature) is a fault at the end of a fully loaded cable — the least current the device will ever see, and the figure that proves it trips.
Typically 0.08 for LV multicore. From the manufacturer where it matters.

At the downstream device’s position. The answer changes with it.

What the published curves allow is an upper bound, not a guarantee. Real behaviour at high fault currents depends on let-through energy, which is why manufacturers publish selectivity tables for specific pairs — and why those tables sometimes claim more than the curves do. Where such a table exists, it wins.

The two ends fail independently. An overload is settled by the thermal elements and needs the ratings far enough apart; a short circuit is settled by the magnetic elements and needs the fault to stay below the upstream device’s instantaneous pickup. A pair can pass one and fail the other.
β from the datasheet. Negative on every silicon module — typically −0,25 to −0,35.

Cells run well above air temperature in sun; 70 °C is ordinary on a roof.
The site's record low, not its average winter. This is the case that damages inverters.

Cell temperature is asked for rather than derived from air temperature. The relationship depends on mounting, ventilation and irradiance, and guessing it would put a large unstated approximation inside a limit that has to be respected exactly.

The maximum is a destruction limit, not a performance one. A string sized on the nameplate 25 °C voltage exceeds the inverter on the first cold clear morning — open circuit, before the inverter has started.
This sizes the string by voltage only. Module current against the inverter's input rating, and the string count against its total power, are separate checks.
The minimum is only a production limit: fall under the MPPT window on a hot afternoon and the array stops earning, which is expensive but not destructive.
The maximum rounds down and the minimum rounds up. One module too many is the damaging direction; one too few only stops the string tracking.

A design convention, not a code figure — see the notes

Which limit binds depends on how the cables lie. Four 20 mm cables across a 100 mm tray take 80 % of its width but only 21 % of its cross-section — an area percentage alone would call that tray four fifths empty when nothing more can be laid in it.
The depth figure assumes ideal packing, so treat it as a lower bound — round cables in a real tray sit looser than that.

Geometry is not the usual failure. A tray is rated in kg per metre of span, and a full tray of copper reaches that long before it looks full. Total the cable weights and check them against the tray's rated load and support spacing.

Power cables are normally laid in a single layer so each can shed heat to the air. Stacking them is what forces the grouping derating up, and a tray that passes on area can still be a thermal problem.

Spacing is not decoration. IEC 60364-5-52 gives a noticeably better grouping factor for cables separated by one diameter than for cables in contact, which is why designs often pay for the extra tray width to get the ampacity back.

IEC 61537 is a product standard for cable tray systems: it classifies safe working load, span and corrosion resistance, and sets no fill percentage. NEC 392.22 does regulate fill, but by absolute area allowances that depend on tray width and cable size rather than by a percentage. The figure here is a design convention and is yours to change.

Primary and secondary currents are in inverse proportion to the voltage ratio, which is the ampere-turns balance of an ideal transformer. Magnetising current and losses are neglected.
Transformers are rated in apparent power (kVA), not active power (kW). Their limit is set by current and voltage, so the load's power factor does not change the full load current.

The short-circuit figures assume an infinite upstream network — zero supply impedance behind the transformer. Real networks add impedance, so the actual fault current is lower. This makes the value conservative for selecting switchgear breaking capacity, but it is not the figure to use when verifying that a protective device will trip.
For three phase, both voltages are line-to-line values and the currents are line currents.
The result is the symmetrical RMS fault current. Peak asymmetrical current, which sets the electrodynamic withstand requirement, is higher and must be derived separately.

Enter the one-way route length. The factor of 2 (DC and single phase) or √3 (three phase) already accounts for the return path and the line-to-line reference.
Limits follow IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G: 3 % for lighting and 5 % for other uses, measured from the origin of the installation.

Conductor reactance is neglected. This is the standard simplified method and is accurate where resistance dominates (roughly up to 16 mm²). For larger conductors, reactance adds to the drop — use the manufacturer's mV/A/m data instead.

Resistivity is corrected to the conductor operating temperature. A copper conductor at 70 °C is about 20 % more resistive than at 20 °C, so calculating at ambient under-reports the drop by the same margin.
